\begin{document}

\title{TRACE-IDS: Cross-Dataset Intrusion Detection\\Fails Zero-Shot, Recovered by Few-Shot}
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Rijan Rayamajhi}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Independent Researcher\\ rayamajhirijan5051@gmail.com}}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Machine-learning intrusion detectors reach near-perfect scores when trained and tested on one
dataset, but deployment means running on a network the model never saw. We evaluate this transfer
directly on two standardized NetFlow v3 datasets (NF-CICIDS2018 and NF-UNSW-NB15, 47 shared
features). Zero-shot transfer fails completely: a Random Forest with 0.95 in-dataset F1 detects
\emph{zero} attacks on the other dataset (cross-dataset recall 0.00), and its 0.96 ``accuracy'' is
an artifact of class imbalance. Per-dataset feature alignment, balanced class weights, and
explanation-guided feature selection do not fix it. The practical fix is cheap supervision: adding
five labeled examples per class from the target network recovers 0.88 attack recall, ten give 0.93,
and fifty give 0.99. Cross-dataset detection therefore needs a small, recurring amount of target
labeling for each new network, and we quantify how little.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
intrusion detection, cross-dataset generalization, few-shot learning, transfer learning, NetFlow
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Most machine-learning intrusion detectors are judged on one dataset: train on it, test on it,
report F1 above 0.95. Deployment is not like that. A real detector meets traffic from a network it
never trained on. We test that directly and find the benchmark numbers do not survive it: a Random
Forest trained on NF-CICIDS2018 scores 0.95 F1 in-dataset, then catches \emph{zero} attacks on
NF-UNSW-NB15.

The usual repairs do not help. Rescaling each dataset to a common range, weighting the minority
class, and selecting ``transferable'' features by SHAP all leave cross-dataset recall at zero. A
little target data helps: a handful of labeled flows from the new network restores most of the
detection, and we measure how many are needed.

\begin{itemize}
\item On standardized NetFlow v3 data we show zero-shot cross-dataset detection fails outright
(recall 0.00), and that accuracy hides this because the target is 96\% benign.
\item We show alignment, balanced weights, and invariant-feature selection do not recover it.
\item We quantify a cheap fix: five labeled examples per class give 0.88 recall, ten give 0.93,
and fifty give 0.99, so deployment on a new network needs very little labeling.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
Cross-dataset generalization of ML-NIDS is known to be poor: within-dataset scores above 0.95 fall
toward chance across datasets \cite{crossdataset}. One barrier is that the common benchmarks use
different feature extractors, so a model trained on one cannot even be applied to another. Sarhan
\emph{et al.} addressed this by re-extracting several public datasets into a single standardized
NetFlow schema, which makes a fair cross-dataset comparison possible \cite{netflow}; we use the
version~3 release of that effort. Domain-invariant representation methods try to close the remaining
gap by learning features that transfer between networks \cite{dinids}, and SHAP has been used to
study which features carry across datasets \cite{shapfs}. Few-shot learning is the emerging practical
direction: recent work recovers strong cross-domain accuracy from a handful of labeled target
samples using multi-domain fusion and attention \cite{fewshot}. We contribute a reproducible
measurement on the standardized data with a simple model: the zero-shot failure, the fact that
common fixes do not help, and a few-shot recovery curve.

\section{Method}
\subsection{Datasets}
We use NF-CICIDS2018-v3 and NF-UNSW-NB15-v3 \cite{netflow}. Both share one standardized 55-column
NetFlow schema, so no manual feature mapping is needed. We drop identifier columns (IP addresses,
ports, timestamps, and the attack-category string) because they leak dataset identity and let a
model memorize one network rather than learn attack behavior. That leaves 47 flow-statistic features
(byte and packet counts, durations, TCP flags, inter-arrival-time statistics, throughput) and the
binary label. Rows with infinite or missing values are dropped, and numeric columns are coerced to
floats. NF-CICIDS2018 has about 20M flows, so we subsample it to about 2M for tractability;
NF-UNSW-NB15 is used in full (about 2.2M flows). Both are imbalanced: 13\% of CIC flows are attacks
and only 4\% of UNSW flows are, which is why accuracy alone is misleading on the cross-dataset test.

\subsection{Model and Evaluation}
The detector is a Random Forest (200 trees, fixed random seed, balanced class weights). It trains on
70\% of CIC and is evaluated on the held-out 30\% (same-dataset) and on all of UNSW (cross-dataset).
Because the target is heavily imbalanced, we report attack recall and F1 rather than accuracy: a
model that labels everything benign scores 0.96 accuracy on UNSW while detecting nothing. The fixed
seed makes every number reproducible from the released code.

\subsection{Alignment and Invariant-Feature Selection}
We test two common repairs. Per-dataset alignment z-scores each dataset by its own training mean and
standard deviation, so the features occupy a comparable range without sharing statistics across
datasets. Explanation-guided invariant-feature selection computes SHAP importance for a CIC-trained
and a UNSW-trained model and keeps features that are important in both datasets and push the label in
the same direction, measured by the sign of the attack-minus-benign mean; the detector then retrains
on that subset.

\subsection{Few-Shot Recovery}
We add $k$ labeled flows per class, drawn from a target pool, to the source training set and retrain,
then evaluate on a fixed held-out target test set. $k=0$ is the zero-shot case. Both datasets are
z-scored by their own statistics so they share a comparable space, and the target test set is never
used for training at any $k$.

\section{Results and Discussion}
Table~\ref{tab:cross} reports the zero-shot results. In-dataset F1 is 0.95, but cross-dataset recall
is 0.00 for every configuration: the detector labels all UNSW traffic benign and catches no attacks.
Its 0.96 cross-dataset ``accuracy'' is purely the benign fraction. Alignment changes nothing,
balanced weights do not rescue recall, and invariant-feature selection only lowers accuracy without
raising recall.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Zero-shot transfer, NF-CICIDS2018 $\rightarrow$ NF-UNSW-NB15. Recall is attack detection.}
\label{tab:cross}
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Configuration & same F1 & cross recall & cross F1 & cross acc \\
\midrule
No alignment (raw)              & 0.95 & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.96 \\
Per-dataset alignment           & 0.95 & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.96 \\
Alignment + invariant selection & 0.93 & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.29 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Figure~\ref{fig:shap} shows why. The features the model relies on differ between the two datasets.
TTL-based features (MIN\_TTL, MAX\_TTL) and packet-size features (SHORTEST\_FLOW\_PKT,
MIN\_IP\_PKT\_LEN) dominate, but their ranking and scale are not the same across datasets, so a
boundary learned on CIC lands in the wrong place on UNSW. This is a distribution-shift problem, not a
capacity problem: the same model fits each dataset well on its own.

The mismatch runs deeper than feature scale. The two datasets come from different testbeds with
different attack taxonomies \cite{netflow}. UNSW-NB15 traffic covers nine attack families: fuzzers,
analysis, backdoors, DoS, exploits, generic, reconnaissance, shellcode, and worms. CICIDS2018
instead contains brute-force, DoS, DDoS, web attacks, infiltration, and botnet traffic. The two sets
overlap only in part, so many attack behaviors the model could learn from one never appear in the
other. A classifier that has seen CICIDS2018 floods and botnet beacons has no template for UNSW
exploit or fuzzer flows, which is one reason zero-shot recall drops to zero. Few-shot labeling helps
because a few target examples give the model its first look at the families it is missing.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{shap_importance.png}
\caption{Per-dataset SHAP feature importance (top 15). The features the model leans on differ
between datasets, which is why a source-only model does not transfer.}
\label{fig:shap}
\end{figure}

Table~\ref{tab:fewshot} and Figure~\ref{fig:fewshot} show the fix. Five labeled examples per class
from the target network raise attack recall from 0.00 to 0.88, ten give 0.93, and fifty give 0.99.
Recall climbs first and precision follows: at $k=5$ recall is already 0.88 while F1 is only 0.37, so
the model catches most attacks but raises many false alarms; by $k=50$ F1 reaches 0.99 as precision
catches up. The curve saturates quickly, so a few dozen labeled flows per class are enough.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Few-shot recovery on NF-UNSW-NB15. $k$ is labeled target flows per class.}
\label{tab:fewshot}
\centering
\begin{tabular}{rccc}
\toprule
$k$ & recall & F1 & accuracy \\
\midrule
0   & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.96 \\
1   & 0.18 & 0.25 & 0.96 \\
5   & 0.88 & 0.37 & 0.88 \\
10  & 0.93 & 0.65 & 0.96 \\
50  & 0.99 & 0.99 & 1.00 \\
100 & 0.99 & 1.00 & 1.00 \\
500 & 1.00 & 1.00 & 1.00 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fewshot.png}
\caption{Few-shot recovery. Zero-shot recall is 0.00; a handful of labeled target flows per class
restores detection: 0.88 recall at five samples per class, 0.93 at ten, 0.99 at fifty.}
\label{fig:fewshot}
\end{figure}

The takeaway is practical for deployment. Attack signatures differ too much between networks for a
source-only model to reuse, so some target labeling is unavoidable. A few labeled flows per class on
the new network are enough to redeploy a working detector, without relabeling everything.

\section{Limitations}
The study uses two datasets and one model, so the numbers show what is possible rather than a tuned
upper bound. Evaluation is offline on captured flows, with no real-time or adversarial testing, and
the few-shot samples are drawn uniformly, not by an active-learning policy that a deployment could
use to label fewer flows. The SHAP analysis explains the failure qualitatively; it does not yet
drive the feature selection, which did not help here.

\section{Conclusion}
On standardized NetFlow v3 data, zero-shot cross-dataset intrusion detection fails completely, and
feature alignment, balanced weights, and invariant-feature selection do not fix it. Few-shot labeling
does: five to fifty labeled examples per class recover 0.88 to 0.99 attack recall. Future work is to
extend this to a leave-one-dataset-out benchmark across the four standardized NetFlow datasets, to
choose the few-shot samples by active learning, and to test deeper models.
